summary: Describes how to use XCAP to manipulate the contents of presence documents based on PIDF in SIP-based presence systems, letting a user manually set parts of their published presence information.

plainLanguage.summary: Presence is your status: online, busy, away. This describes using XCAP so a user can edit parts of that status directly on the server.

questions: how to change presence document contents
xcap vs sip publish for presence
where is an xcap presence document stored
subtitle: Lets a user store a permanent presence document on a server with XCAP, alongside the temporary state devices publish with SIP.

tldr.problem: SIP PUBLISH creates soft state that expires unless a device keeps refreshing it, so it cannot express presence that should stay put when no device is active, such as a vacation.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines an XCAP application usage, with the AUID pidf-manipulation, so clients can read and write one PIDF presence document per user on an XCAP server, which feeds the event state compositor as one more input.
tldr.outcome: A user can set persistent, device-independent presence state that the compositor combines with whatever SIP PUBLISH sources report.

facts.label: Documents per user
facts.value: One, named index under the users tree

today: RFC 4827 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the XCAP specification in RFC 4825.

sections.title: Introduction and the Gap in SIP PUBLISH
sections.content:
In SIP-based presence, a watcher subscribes to a presentity to learn its presence information. A Presence User Agent (PUA) can publish its own view of the presence state with the SIP PUBLISH method, without learning about the states set by other PUAs.

The catch is that PUBLISH creates soft state. It expires after the negotiated lifetime unless it is refreshed, so it does not suit cases where the state should stay without an active device to refresh it.

RFC 4827 names three such cases: setting person-related state while no device is active (traveling, vacations), setting state for services that are open even if no device runs them (e-mail, MMS, SMS), and setting a default state for a person, service or device when nothing is publishing. The document says SIP PUBLISH remains the main way to publish dynamic presence state and that this mechanism complements it.
sections.plainLanguage: A status that a device sets fades away unless the device keeps repeating it. If you are away on holiday with no devices on, you need a note that stays put by itself.

sections.title: Why XCAP Fits
sections.content:
The XML Configuration Access Protocol (XCAP) lets a client read, write and modify application configuration data stored as XML on a server. The data has no expiration time, so it has to be explicitly inserted and deleted. Several clients can change the same data as long as they are authorized.

XCAP is already used in SIMPLE-based presence systems for presence lists and presence authorization policies. The RFC therefore treats it as an ideal choice for device-independent presence document manipulation.

The document format is the Presence Information Data Format (PIDF). It is used because the event state compositor already has to support PIDF for SIP PUBLISH.
sections.plainLanguage: XCAP is like a shared notebook on a server. Whatever you write stays until you erase it, and any of your devices that is allowed in can edit it.

sections.title: How It Fits with SIP PUBLISH
sections.content:
The event state compositor combines presence information from several sources into one coherent presence document. The XCAP-manipulated document is one source. Soft state published with SIP PUBLISH is another. Normally there can be several PUAs publishing separate views, but only a single XCAP-manipulated presence document.

Many XCAP clients, for example on different devices, may edit that one document on the XCAP server, but it still counts as a single input. The two kinds of input are completely separate: neither mechanism can directly change the state set by the other.

How the compositor treats XCAP-based input relative to PUBLISH-based input is compositor policy and out of scope. The RFC adds no new requirements for the compositor, since the PUBLISH specification already requires it to build overall state from inputs that may be non-orthogonal or even conflicting. The protocol between the XCAP server and the compositor is not specified.
sections.plainLanguage: A referee collects reports from your devices and one permanent note, then writes the final status. The note and the device reports cannot edit each other.

sections.title: The Application Usage Definition
sections.content:
XCAP requires every application usage to define a set of properties. This RFC fills them in as follows.

  • AUID: pidf-manipulation, in the IETF tree, registered with IANA.
  • MIME type: application/pidf+xml.
  • Schema: the PIDF XML Schema and its extensions. The PIDF namespace URI urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:pidf is also the XCAP default document namespace.
  • Constraints and interdependencies: none beyond those in PIDF and XCAP.
  • Naming: the server MUST store only a single XCAP-manipulated presence document for each user, located under the users tree with the filename index.
  • Authorization: the default XCAP policy is unchanged, so only the owner may read, write or modify their documents. A server can let privileged users modify others' documents, but how is outside the scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules say: use one special label for this kind of note, keep exactly one note per person under the same file name, and let only the owner edit it.

sections.title: Example: Away on Vacation
sections.content:
The RFC's example is a person who has left on vacation and set presence so they are only available by e-mail. With no published soft state, this document would be the sole input to the compositor.

The user is the SIP address sip:someone@example.com, the XCAP root is http://xcap.example.com, and the XCAP user identifier equals the SIP address. The document lives at /pidf-manipulation/users/sip:someone@example.com/index. It is created with an HTTP PUT. It holds a closed tuple for a SIP contact, an open tuple for a mailto: contact with a note, and a person element showing a vacation activity, using the RPID and CIPID extensions.

To change just the e-mail note, the client sends a PUT to a node selector under ~~/presence/tuple[@id='x8eg92n']/note, with an If-Match header and the content type application/xcap-el+xml. Only that element is replaced.
sections.plainLanguage: You write on the notice board that you are on holiday and only reachable by e-mail. Later you can fix just one line instead of rewriting the whole board.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A presence document may contain highly sensitive information. It must reach watchers strictly according to the relevant authorization policies, and only authorized clients may change it.

The XCAP base specification requires every XCAP server to implement HTTP Digest authentication (RFC 2617) and HTTP over TLS (RFC 2818). The RFC recommends that administrators use an HTTPS URI as the XCAP root services URI, so that digest authentication happens over TLS. Together these give confidentiality and integrity for the operations and ensure that only authorized clients can perform them.
sections.plainLanguage: Your status can be private, so only you get to edit the note, and the connection to the notebook is locked so nobody can read or swap it on the way.

viz.caption: TWO INPUTS TO THE EVENT STATE COMPOSITOR

cells: Soft state that expires unless refreshed
No expiration; explicitly inserted and deleted
Several PUAs, each with its own view

viz.caption: UPDATING ONE ELEMENT (FROM THE RFC EXAMPLE)

data.title: XCAP PUT to change the e-mail note
data.code:
PUT /pidf-manipulation/users/sip:someone@example.com/index/
~~/presence/tuple%5b@id='x8eg92n'%5d/note HTTP/1.1
If-Match: "xyz"
Host: xcap.example.com
Content-Type: application/xcap-el+xml

<note>I'm reading mails on Tuesdays and Fridays</note>
